passage: Gurleen first noticed it at the dinner table in their Lajpat Nagar flat. Her cousin Tenzin, who had lived with them since starting college, called his old friends "sleepers" and the group's founder "the Guide." When Gurleen asked what that meant, he smiled as if she were a child. By October he had stopped going to his evening classes. His phone was always face down, and he left the room for calls. One night she heard him on the balcony saying, "I know, I shouldn't have asked. I'll accept the correction." His best friend from school rang the landline looking for him; Tenzin told Gurleen to say he was out. The next morning she saw a printed list on his desk titled "People who hold you back." Her own name was on it. Gurleen sat on her bed for a long time, then went to find her mother.

qa.q: What did Tenzin call the group's founder?
qa.a: He called the group's founder the Guide.

qa.q: How does Gurleen feel when she sees her own name on the list?
qa.a: Gurleen feels hurt and frightened, because she can see Tenzin is being pushed to cut off the people who care about him.

qa.q: What turning point can the family use at this stage?
qa.a: Gurleen and her mother can talk calmly together about the signs, keep warm contact with Tenzin without mocking the group, and look for advice from a counsellor who knows about high-control groups.

qa.q: What might Tenzin be experiencing when he says he will accept the correction?
qa.a: He may feel ashamed and afraid for having asked a question, because the group seems to punish doubt.

grounding: Shows a family member noticing a relative's secrecy, group jargon, dropped studies and friends, punishment for questions and pressure to cut ties.

passage:
First Saturday: Vishal had moved to Pune for his first job and knew no one. At a free "mindful living" evening, twelve people hugged him at the door and invited him to a weekend retreat. He loved it, and felt a little dizzy with it.
Following Wednesday: on a video call, Afreen, his friend from college, asked who ran it. Vishal realised he didn't know. So at the next meet-up he asked the organiser three things: where the retreat fees went, who the leaders answered to, and what happened if someone wanted to stop coming. The organiser's smile tightened. "Those are outsider questions. Trust takes time."
Two Sundays later: Vishal compared that with the running club he had also joined, where the treasurer showed him the accounts and a member said, "Come when you like, skip when you like." He kept running on Sundays, and he kept calling Afreen.

qa.q: What three things did Vishal ask the organiser?
qa.a: He asked where the retreat fees went, who the leaders answered to, and what happened if someone wanted to stop coming.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel at the first mindful living evening?
qa.a: He felt welcomed and happy after being alone in a new city, though the hugs and quick invitation also left him a little dizzy.

qa.q: Which choice protected Vishal, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking plain questions about money, leaders and leaving, and staying in touch with Afreen, let him see which group welcomed questions and which went cold.

qa.q: How might Afreen see the part that one video call played?
qa.a: Afreen might feel relieved that one simple question on a video call helped Vishal look more carefully, and glad Vishal still calls.

grounding: Shows a lonely young adult asking about a group's money, leaders and exit rules and staying close to outside friends, comparing a group that resists questions with one that welcomes them.

[Sunday, 10:12 pm]
Charu: Bhaiya, don't start. I know you think they're a cult
Jagdish: I didn't say that. I just miss you. Mummy made rajma today, your plate was empty 🙂
Charu: they said you'd use food to guilt me
Jagdish: Fair. No guilt. Can I ask something real though?
Charu: what
Jagdish: What does the group give you that you weren't getting from us?
Charu: ...
Charu: they listen. nobody at home ever asked what I think about anything
Jagdish: That's true. I didn't. I'm sorry for that.
Charu: you're not going to argue?
Jagdish: No. I want to know more. What do you like best there?
Charu: the morning circle. people say what they feel
Jagdish: That sounds good. Could we do a small version, you and me, one call a week?
Charu: maybe. don't tell Mummy I said that
Jagdish: I'll just tell her you're okay. Love you, pagli ❤️

qa.q: What did Mummy make that day?
qa.a: Mummy made rajma, and Charu's plate was empty.

qa.q: What does Charu's question, you're not going to argue?, suggest Charu was expecting?
qa.a: It suggests Charu was braced and defensive, expecting ridicule, and is surprised and a little softened when Jagdish just listens.

qa.q: What turning point does Jagdish create, and what could he keep doing?
qa.a: He asks open questions and admits the family's gap instead of arguing, and he can keep a weekly call so a path back stays open.

qa.q: What would change if Jagdish had called the group a cult in the chat?
qa.a: Charu would likely feel the group's warning had come true, go quiet, and trust Jagdish less.

grounding: Shows a family member staying affectionate, avoiding ridicule and asking what the group gives, which keeps the connection open.

passage: In the shared house outside Lisbon, the rule was that everyone gave their weekend to the movement's bookshop. Sofia had given two years of weekends. Last Friday the leaders announced that Thabo, who had worked there longest, was "stepping away to reflect" after he asked why the donations never appeared in the accounts. Sofia had wondered the same thing for months. She said nothing at the meeting. Nobody did. That night she lay awake listening to the trams, rehearsing a question and then imagining the room turning to look at her. If she left, who would she even have? The leaders said the world outside was cruel to people like them. At breakfast she smiled, passed the bread, and felt guilty for the thought she had not spoken. By Sunday her jaw ached from clenching it in her sleep.

qa.q: Why was Thabo stepping away, according to the passage?
qa.a: He asked why the donations never appeared in the accounts, and the leaders announced he was stepping away to reflect.

qa.q: What was Sofia feeling as she lay awake listening to the trams?
qa.a: Sofia felt anxious and afraid, torn between her own doubts about the money and fear of losing everyone if she spoke.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Sofia now?
qa.a: Sofia could quietly contact Thabo or someone outside the house she trusts, so her doubts are not held alone, and look for a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Thabo be feeling after being sent away?
qa.a: Thabo may feel punished and isolated for asking a fair question, and perhaps unsure whether anyone inside agreed with him.

grounding: Shows a member noticing unfair treatment and a money contradiction but keeping silent out of fear and shame, with anxiety, sleeplessness and guilt.

subtopic: Drawn into a high-control group or online extremism
passage: Elizabeth waited for Farida outside the metro station in Andheri, holding two cutting chais. It had been five months. Farida arrived in a plain grey kurta, hair tied back tightly, and took the tea without sipping it. "You look tired," Elizabeth said gently. "I'm fine. Growth is tiring," Farida replied, as if reading from a card. Elizabeth asked about the weekend sessions. "People who aren't inside can't judge it." Elizabeth's cheeks burned. She wanted to say that her friend had missed her own sister's wedding. She wanted to say the word "cult." She took a slow breath instead. "Okay. I'm not judging. I just missed you." Farida looked at her for a second, then down at her phone. "I have to go." Elizabeth nodded. "Same place next month? No questions, just chai." Farida didn't answer, but she didn't say no.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth holding outside the metro station?
qa.a: She was holding two cutting chais.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when Farida said people outside can't judge it?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt hurt and frustrated, with burning cheeks and the urge to argue, but she chose to stay calm.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth's approach do well at this stage?
qa.a: By not using the word cult and offering another meeting with no questions, she kept a safe door open for when Farida's doubts grow.

qa.q: How might Farida see the invitation for next month?
qa.a: Farida may feel wary and defensive, yet the fact that she doesn't say no suggests some part of her wants the friendship to stay.

grounding: Shows a friend who reaches out meeting a stock, defensive reply and choosing calm and an open door over ridicule.

I'm Ramesh. It's been eight months since I walked out of the centre, and some evenings I still miss the singing more than anything. That's the strange part: I grieve people who told me my family was poison. I'm also ashamed of things I said at my father's table back then, how sure I was.
The counsellor told me not to rush. So I'm relearning small things. Last week I realised I don't actually like the plain rice diet we all ate; I like my mother's fish curry, extra sour. I started going to a Sunday quiz at a café with Arnab from work. He laughs at everything, argues about cricket, and doesn't need me to agree with him. My sister comes over on Fridays now. Some days I still hear the old rules in my head. They're getting quieter.

qa.a: Ramesh goes to a Sunday quiz at a café with Arnab from work.

passage:
Note by the class teacher, Class 10B, Friday
Himani has been quieter since the inter-school quiz selection. She topped the trials, but the place went to a student whose parent is on the school committee. I believe she has a real point, and I said so to the coordinator.
This week, in free period, Siddharth mentioned that Himani watches a creator who posts long videos about "rigged systems" and "people like us who never get a chance." Today, in the essay on fairness, she quoted him twice. She looked almost lighter while writing, as if someone finally understood her.
What I did next: I asked Himani to stay back and told her the selection had been unfair and she was right to be angry. I asked what the videos said that felt true. She talked for ten minutes. I have asked the counsellor to meet her next week, and I've called her mother to share what I noticed.

qa.q: Who mentioned the videos Himani watches?
qa.a: Siddharth mentioned that Himani watches a creator who posts long videos about rigged systems.

qa.q: How does Himani seem to feel when she quotes the videos in her essay?
qa.a: She seems relieved and understood, looking almost lighter, because the videos voice the anger she feels about the unfair selection.

qa.q: What turning point does the teacher use, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: The teacher first admits the grievance is real, then listens to what feels true in the videos, which keeps Himani talking instead of pushing her further toward the creator.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel about having mentioned the videos?
qa.a: Siddharth may feel a little uneasy about talking behind Himani's back but also relieved that an adult is paying attention.

grounding: Shows a teenager with a partly true grievance finding online content that voices her anger and feeling relieved to be understood.

passage:
My name is Minakshi, and this happened in the summer before Class 11. I clicked one video about the fee hike at our coaching centre. It was angry and funny, and I watched it twice. By the next day my whole feed was fee hikes, then "useless teachers," then "this generation is being robbed." I remember thinking, wow, everyone is furious, not just me.
I posted a small comment and got forty likes. So the next one was sharper. I called a teacher a fraud; two hundred likes. My chest would buzz every time the number went up. Devika, my best friend, sent me a normal video of her cat, and I felt nothing. It seemed so small compared to my important anger. Looking back, I can see I had stopped scrolling for news. I was scrolling for that buzz.

qa.q: How many likes did Minakshi's first small comment get?
qa.a: Minakshi's first small comment got forty likes.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling each time the likes went up?
qa.a: Minakshi felt a thrilling buzz of excitement and importance, which made the anger feel rewarding.

qa.q: What turning point could Minakshi have used at that point in the summer?
qa.a: Minakshi could have noticed that the posts were getting harsher for likes, taken a break from the feed, and talked it over with Devika or a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt when her cat video got no reply?
qa.a: Devika may have felt ignored and puzzled, sensing her best friend was drifting into something that left no room for ordinary things.

grounding: Shows a teenager clicking angry content until the feed feels like the whole world, with outrage rewarded by likes and posts getting harsher.

passage: I'm Pankaj, Pooja's older brother, so I sit across from her at dinner every night. For most of last term she'd scroll with this tight face and then read us some furious post about our town council. Then, after a computer class on how apps choose what you see, something changed. I saw her go through her follows one evening, tapping "mute" again and again. She said, "This guy posts the same outrage every day. It's built to make me angry." A few days later she was reading two news pages on the same council vote, one each side, and asking me which bits I believed. Last week a post about the council made her grip the phone. She put it down, went for water, and came back. I can't say what she felt inside. She just didn't share it.

qa.q: What did Pooja tap again and again one evening?
qa.a: She went through her follows tapping mute again and again.

qa.q: What does Pooja putting the phone down and going for water suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt a flash of anger but chose to pause and calm herself before reacting to a post designed to provoke her.

qa.q: What skill has Pooja built that Pankaj or others could learn from?
qa.a: She now notices when a post is built to anger her, mutes rage accounts and reads more than one side before deciding what to believe.

qa.q: How has dinner changed for Pankaj since last term?
qa.a: Pankaj no longer has to hear furious posts read out every night, and instead Pooja asks him what he believes, which feels more like a real conversation.

grounding: Shows a teen learning how feeds are tuned to provoke, muting rage accounts, following sources from more than one side and pausing before reacting.
